common_name: Earth Angel Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Wide Creamy-Gold Margin)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; the wide gold margin colors best with some morning light but needs afternoon shade to avoid scorch.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Earth Angel is a large, award-winning hosta with heavily corrugated, blue-green leaves edged in a wide, irregular creamy-gold margin that widens further as the clump matures, one of the boldest variegation patterns among big hostas. The American Hosta Society named it Hosta of the Year in 2010 for its outstanding vigor, substance, and garden performance. Near-white flowers appear on tall scapes in mid to late summer, though the plant's real draw is its season-long foliage display as a specimen or anchor for a large shaded bed. Divide only when necessary, since large hostas like this one take several seasons to reach full, dramatic size.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; protect from afternoon sun in zone 8–9 to keep the white margin from scorching.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Whirlwind bears twisted, wavy-margined leaves with a green center and a crisp white edge, the distinctive twist giving the clump an animated, swirling texture unlike the flatter-leaved hostas around it. It is a moderately vigorous grower that increases into a well-formed mound over a few seasons. Pale lavender flowers rise on scapes in mid to late summer above the foliage. Divide congested clumps in early spring as new growth emerges, and site it where its unusual twisted form can be viewed up close along a path or bed edge.

common_name: Substantial Evidence Daylily (Heavily Ruffled Cream-Gold Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; the heavy ruffling and substance of this cultivar develop best with consistent moisture and a full day of light.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Substantial Evidence produces large, extremely thick-substanced, heavily ruffled cream-to-gold flowers with a lightly gold-edged ruffle, bred to hold their crisp form through the heat of the day when thinner-petaled daylilies wilt or go limp by afternoon. Vigorous branched scapes carry numerous buds, extending bloom over several weeks rather than a single flush. Remove spent scapes after flowering to keep the clump tidy and channel energy back into the crown. Divide every three to four years in spring as the clump becomes congested, watering divisions well until re-established.

common_name: Vanity Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Clear Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced in the early 1970s and a Dykes Medal winner, Vanity bears tall, softly ruffled, clear rose-pink flowers of exceptional form and substance on strong branched stems, and its clean, unfading pink long made it a benchmark for pink bearded iris breeding. It remains a vigorous, floriferous grower decades after introduction, valued for reliable rebloom of full stalks year after year rather than novelty coloring. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting healthy outer fans; good drainage is essential to prevent rot.

common_name: Before the Storm Bearded Iris (Near-Black Velvet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun. Before the Storm is one of the most popular near-black bearded iris in commerce, its deep purple-black, velvety falls and standards reading as almost pure black in bright sun, with a subtle sheen that catches the light differently through the day. It is a vigorous, reliable grower and multiplies readily into a full clump within a few seasons. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting healthy outer fans spaced to allow air movement and reduce rot risk.
